full-metal-jacket-1987.gazette: R. Lee Ermey joined the production as a technical advisor and ended up cast as Gunnery Sergeant Hartman. He had done the job for real in the Marine Corps, and much of what he delivers on screen is drill-instructor procedure rather than screenwriting — the cadence, the inventory of insults, the timing between them. Kubrick built the first half of the film around that accuracy: not a portrait of cruelty, but a schedule for producing it.

slacker-1990.gazette: Linklater filled the cast with people he already knew in Austin, non-actors delivering versions of their own talk and their own theories. The camera hands off from one to the next and never comes back, so the city rather than a protagonist becomes the thing being recorded. The contract is social realism at street level: these were the conversations happening in that town at the end of the eighties.

la-belle-noiseuse-1991.gazette: The hand that draws in the long unbroken takes belongs to Bernard Dufour, a working painter, not to Michel Piccoli. Rivette kept the camera on paper for minutes at a stretch while charcoal actually crossed it, which is why the marks accumulate at the speed of labour instead of the speed of montage. The film's central claim is procedural: the picture on screen was made while the film was being made.
la-belle-noiseuse-1991.prism: That choice costs the film its star at exactly the point where a star would normally do the work. Piccoli plays the artist everywhere except at the easel — the one place the film decided could not be acted.

through-the-olive-trees-1994.gazette: Kiarostami went back to Koker after the 1990 earthquake and cast the people living in the rubble as the people living in the rubble. The film restages the making of his own previous picture on that ground, so the crew, the auditions and a local boy pursuing a local girl all sit at the same level of reality. Fiction and record are not layered here; they are shot on the same hillside, in the same hour.

the-white-balloon-1995.gazette: Panahi's first feature runs close to real time, tracking the last stretch of hours before the Iranian New Year as a seven-year-old tries to buy a goldfish. The lead had never acted, and the streets were Tehran's own — shopkeepers, soldiers, a snake charmer, a balloon seller, all at their ordinary distance from the child. Nothing in the plot ever exceeds the value of a single banknote, and the film holds that scale for its full length.

christmas-in-august-1998.gazette: Hur Jin-ho built his debut around a small neighbourhood photo studio and kept the camera at a customer's distance from it. The dying man's illness is never announced and never diagnosed on screen; it arrives through routine instead — shop hours, a father being taught to work a remote control, film handed over a counter. Korean melodrama's loudest register was fully available in 1998, and the film declined it.
christmas-in-august-1998.prism: Restraint that complete moves the work onto the audience: nobody in the frame explains what is happening, so noticing becomes the viewer's job. It's a realism contract that only pays out if you're watching the routine, because the routine is the entire event.

platform-2001.gazette: Jia followed a state performing troupe in provincial Shanxi across roughly a decade of the reform era, from Mao-period repertoire to privatised pop tours. The takes run long and hold back, so political change enters the frame the way it entered the province — through haircuts, cassette players, flared trousers, and the slow rewriting of what a job is. The troupe's contract changes hands; the camera simply keeps running.

distant-2002.gazette: Ceylan shot in his own Istanbul flat through a heavy winter, with a small cast drawn largely from people close to him. The younger man arrives from the village looking for work on the ships, part of the internal migration that had been filling the city for decades, and the film gives him nothing but time on a sofa. Snow falls across the Bosphorus; the ships do not hire.

ten-2002.gazette: Kiarostami fixed two small digital cameras to a car dashboard and largely got out of the vehicle. Ten conversations follow — a driver and her son, a bride, a woman leaving a shrine, a sex worker in the dark — carried by a non-professional cast working without conventional script pages. The whole apparatus is a windscreen, two lenses and Tehran traffic.
ten-2002.prism: Taking the director out of the car also takes away the usual alibi: nobody is being framed by a man standing behind the camera. What replaces him is a machine that never blinks, which turns out to be its own kind of pressure on the woman who has to keep driving.

nobody-knows-2004.gazette: The shoot ran about a year and moved in sequence, so the children visibly age inside the frame — hair longer, sleeves shorter, voices lower. Underneath it is a real case: children left alone in a Tokyo apartment in the late 1980s, unregistered, unenrolled, unnoticed for months. Kore-eda's young cast had not acted before, and the film never once raises its voice about any of it.

the-world-2004.gazette: The setting is an actual place — a Beijing theme park where migrant workers perform as dancers and stand guard beside a scaled Eiffel Tower and a small Manhattan skyline. Jia drew his cast largely from outside the profession and let the long takes show the labour: costume changes, dormitory beds, phone calls home to Shanxi. The park's slogan promises the world without leaving the city; the staff supply the world and stay put.

offside-2006.gazette: Panahi filmed during an actual World Cup qualifier, working in and around the stadium while the match was played and the crowd behaved as crowds behave. His cast were non-professionals and the story runs roughly the length of a game: girls caught trying to enter a ground women were barred from, penned within earshot of the noise. The finished film was banned in Iran.
offside-2006.prism: Shooting live meant the film had no control over its own ending — whatever happened on the pitch was going to be the ending. That was the trade: the ban was the predictable part, the score wasn't.

still-life-2006.gazette: Fengjie was being taken apart while Jia filmed in it, buildings knocked down by hand and wall markers showing where the reservoir would eventually sit. He cast locals and demolition workers, kept the dialect, and moved his fiction through a place that would no longer exist by the time audiences saw it. A man searches for the wife who left him; behind him the town comes down floor by floor.

once-2007.gazette: Long lenses did most of the work in Dublin: Carney's crew filmed from across the road, close enough to catch a busker's take and far enough that the street kept walking past. The leads were musicians rather than actors, and the songs on the soundtrack were their own. This was the city still inside the boom — a hoover repair shop by day, a pitch on Grafton Street by night.

gomorrah-2008.gazette: Garrone adapted Roberto Saviano's investigation and shot it where the material came from, in the Scampia housing blocks of Naples, with local non-professionals through much of the cast. Five strands run in parallel: a money runner, a tailor working a couture supply chain, two teenagers with a stolen arsenal, a waste broker burying toxic loads in the countryside. The book's author had been living under police protection since publication; the film walked into the same territory with a crew.
gomorrah-2008.prism: Filming on the real ground is what gives the thing its authority, and it's also the part nobody can undo afterwards — the crew leaves, the residents stay. The authenticity was borrowed from people who had no other address to move to.
